extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and scientifically-interested laypersons (readers of Popular Science Monthly)
extracted.subtask_description: Short-form popular-science journalism and essays reporting natural-history observations, scientific notes, technical advances, and social-science argumentation for a late-19th-century educated audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize non-natural influences when studying animal habits
rubrics_metrics.description: "While in Africa, the young animal was kept as free as possible from other than natural influences, so that its habits might be studied as accurately as was practicable."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep study subjects as free as possible from artificial/captive influences to observe natural behaviour; design captivity or observation so that human interference is minimized; use such controlled minimal-interference captivity to learn baseline habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare captive and wild behaviour; account for health/context effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed behaviours in captivity may contradict prior reports or disappear when animals are unhealthy or in different conditions (e.g., Mpungu's breast-beating and reelings were seen in Africa but not in Europe because he "never enjoyed good health there").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating animal behaviour, compare observations across contexts (wild, semi-free, captive, differing health states); note how captivity, illness, or environment can suppress or alter natural expressions; avoid generalizing from a single context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specific behavioural instances as evidence of cognitive or affective capacities
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed anecdotes (Chega stuffing cheeks when denied food; bringing down a tablecloth to trap a dog; unhooking a night cord; drumming on hollow things) are used to illustrate faculties like reflection, comparison, cunning, playfulness, shame, or planfulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document precise, repeatable actions and contexts as evidence of cognitive/affective traits; include sequences (intent, action, reaction) and any controls or repeated observations that show the behaviour is characteristic rather than anecdotal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use distributional anatomy and comparative morphology to support botanical hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Polonie suggests pear 'stone-grains' may be rudimentary remnants of a stone casing; evidence includes grains being "thickest in a zone surrounding the seeds" and analogy with related genera whose fruits enclose stones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support morphological/phylogenetic hypotheses by (a) mapping anatomical distribution within organs (e.g., concentration around seeds), (b) assembling series of varieties from minimal to maximal expression, and (c) adducing analogies in related genera; seek graded variation across cultivars/wild types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form graded series across varieties to test evolutionary/developmental hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: By bringing together different cultivated and wild pears one might "arrange a series of fruits in regular gradation, from a luscious pear with hardly any stony grains down to a tough wood-pear" — used as evidence for a vestigial stone casing hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect comparative samples spanning the range of variation; use gradation patterns to infer ancestral traits or morphological reduction; document extreme and intermediate forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify cranial types using cranial indices (transverse/antero-posterior ratios) and comparative series
rubrics_metrics.description: M. Hamy found African populations forming successive groups "from the sub-brachycephalic (moderately short-skulled) to the ... sub-dolichocephalic, and finally to the true dolichocephalic type," i.e., the relation of transverse diameter to antero-posterior diameter diminishes progressively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use measurable cranial indices to distinguish types and map gradations; compare multiple populations, include stature and other metric data, and avoid overgeneralizing from limited samples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess plumbing/material suitability via physical inspection and documented case reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Dr. William Eassie's letter reports lead waste-pipes perforated with 'veritable rat-holes' with clear tooth marks; other specimens showed perforations and corrosion where exposed to decaying wood acids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use physical specimens, photographic/woodcut evidence, and documented case histories to judge material durability and safety; identify exposure conditions (infested drains, contact with decaying wood) that produce failure; draw practical conclusions (e.g., 'lead, where so exposed, is not a safe plumbing material').

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain persistent acoustic phenomena by environmental mechanisms and repeatable tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Reulaux attributes the 'ringing of bells' in a valley to "the passage of the wind through the valley, and modified by its configuration, the character of the rocks, and, probably, by the wood." A forester's horn tone was repeated in the bell-peals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for acoustic phenomena by (a) locating origin and propagation paths in the landscape, (b) testing with known sounds (e.g., horn) to confirm resonance/repetition, and (c) considering geological and vegetative modifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rigid plant/animal dichotomies; classify by observed physiological/functional traits
rubrics_metrics.description: Lecture: 'the animal and vegetable kingdoms could not be separated' — there are plants with movement, sensitivity, digestion-like processes, and animals with minimal organization; distinctions should be empirical rather than categorical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying life-forms use observed traits (movement, sensitivity, digestion, structural organization) and recognize continua; be prepared to revise 'old landmarks' when new precise facts contradict simple dichotomies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate sanitary improvement efficacy with mortality statistics and comparative temporal data
rubrics_metrics.description: Glasgow trustees reported the "average death-rate per one thousand persons has been reduced nearly eleven per cent. in twelve years" after measures like demolition of unwholesome dwellings and provision of hospital space; twelve leading towns had 61,000 fewer deaths in the second six-year period than expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use standardized metrics (death-rate per 1,000), compute percent change over defined time intervals, compare across similar towns, and link observed improvements to implemented interventions (housing removal, hospital capacity, epidemic control). Report absolute and relative changes (e.g., fewer deaths, percent reduction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Document technical experimental/observational parameters for reproducibility (astronomical photography example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Professor Henry Draper reports photographing the nebula near the Trapezium using 'a triple objective of eleven inches aperture, made by Alvan Clark & Sons, and corrected especially for the photographic rays,' with an exposure of fifty minutes and an equatorial stand with a driving clock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For reproducible technical observation, record equipment specs (objective/aperture, optical corrections), exposure durations, and tracking/mounting systems; include intent to publish detailed negatives/description for verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify machine/engine performance with clear efficiency and throughput metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: M. Pifre improved Mouchot's solar engine making 'eighty per cent. available for use' (versus 50% previously); with a 9.25 sq. m receiver he 'boils fifty litres of water in less than forty minutes' and increases pressure by one atmosphere every seven or eight minutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report percent energy utilization, collector/receiver area, work output (e.g., volume boiled, time), and rates of change (pressure per time); compare to prior art and indicate experimental conditions (clear sky).

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe mechanical inventions by explicit working principles and electrical/mechanical parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: The Siemens & Halske rock-drill is described as 'a rod of steel-headed soft iron which moves through three coils of insulated wire; the middle coil is traversed by a constant current which magnetizes the rod, and the other coils are traversed by alternating currents which attract and repel the rod with rapid movements.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting an invention, explain component roles, the nature of currents/forces applied, interaction producing motion, materials used, and how alternating/constant inputs generate the operation; give enough detail to evaluate feasibility and novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comparative ethnographic evidence to infer causes of political differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Spencer argues that political differentiation arises from differential exposure to forces (e.g., sexes exposed to unlike influences become rulers and ruled; habitual war produces slave-classes), illustrating with cross-cultural cases (Chippewas, Clatsops, Chinooks, Bodo, Dhimals, Nootkas, Chinooks, Dyaks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support social-theory claims by assembling comparative cases showing correlation between mode of life (warlike vs peaceful, divisions of labour) and social/political structure; use historical and ethnographic contrasts to make causal inferences but note complexity and intermediate cases.
